stories.title: Lone Star PACE Facilitates Nearly $65M in Loans for 6 Texas Projects
stories.excerpt: Lone Star PACE closed on $64.8 million in Texas PACE Program financing during the first half of 2026, supporting approximately $279 million in commercial real estate investment while helping property owners significantly reduce energy and water consumption. The six closed transactions span a diverse mix of property types, including hospitality, retail, industrial, data centers and specialty development, demonstrating the growing role of Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) financing in helping developers strengthen project capital stacks while incorporating high-performance building systems. Projects financed during the first half of the year include the Holiday Inn Express in Pilot Point, MCM Elegante in Beaumont (shown), Ashford Yard in Houston, Cold Storage Seabrook, Vesgro Data Center in Irving and Maranello Luxury Garages in Plano. The Texas PACE Program enables property owners and developers to finance qualifying energy and water conservation improvements through a voluntary property assessment. C-PACE financing can fund up to 35% of a project’s capital stack and may be used for new construction, redevelopment and retrofit projects. The post Lone Star PACE Facilitates Nearly $65M in Loans for 6 Texas Projects appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Lone Star PACE closed $64.8M in Texas C-PACE financing, supporting $279M investment.
Six projects across hospitality, retail, industrial, data centers, specialty development financed.
C-PACE can fund up to 35% of capital stack for new construction, redevelopment, retrofit.
stories.summary: Lone Star PACE closed $64.8 million in Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy (C-PACE) financing during H1 2026 across six Texas projects, enabling $279 million in total commercial real estate investment. The transactions span hospitality, retail, industrial, data centers, and specialty development. C-PACE financing can fund up to 35% of a project's capital stack and applies to new construction, redevelopment, and retrofit projects.
stories.impact: C-PACE deployment in Texas lowers effective cost of capital for multifamily developers by financing ESG/energy improvements on separate property assessment basis; enables larger equity raises and stronger returns in competitive markets. Watch for increased adoption in Texas submarkets (Houston, Dallas/Irving, Austin) as developers layer C-PACE to offset rising construction and financing costs.

stories.title: Triten Snags Refi on 342-Unit Houston Rental Community
stories.excerpt: Triten Real Estate Partners obtained refinancing for The Mill Residences, a 342-unit mid-rise multifamily community located at 2315 Navigation Blvd. in the East End of Houston, Texas. Northmarq’s Warren Hitchcock and Taylor Phillips arranged the refinance loan on behalf of Triten. Northmarq’s Hitchcock added. “Northmarq secured a creative and flexible refinance prior to final stabilization which replaced the construction loan, provided additional capital for the retail buildout, and gave Triten the runway needed to complete the property’s business plan.” The Mills Residences offers a mix of class A studio, one-, two-bedroom apartments. Amenities such as a fitness center, yoga studio, poolside cabanas and a quiet lounge equipped with high-speed connectivity designed for remote workers. Built in 2025, the multifamily community places residents at the center of Houston’s East End, providing residents with convenient access to public transit, dining, live entertainment and the area’s growing arts district.  The post Triten Snags Refi on 342-Unit Houston Rental Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Triten refinanced 342-unit The Mill Residences, Houston East End, built 2025.
Northmarq structured creative refi pre-stabilization, replaced construction loan, funded retail buildout.
Class A mid-rise with remote-work amenities, transit access, arts district proximity.
stories.summary: Triten Real Estate Partners refinanced The Mill Residences, a 342-unit mid-rise multifamily community completed in 2025 at 2315 Navigation Blvd. in Houston's East End. Northmarq arranged a creative, flexible refinance prior to final stabilization that replaced the construction loan, provided additional capital for retail buildout, and extended runway to complete the business plan. The property offers studio, one-, and two-bedroom units with Class A amenities including fitness center, yoga studio, poolside cabanas, and high-speed connectivity.
stories.impact: Early stabilization-stage refinance signals strong lender appetite for Houston multifamily and willingness to take construction-to-perm risk; indicates robust rental fundamentals in East End submarket. Developers with shovel-ready Houston projects should move forward—capital availability and appetite are improving faster than recent years, reducing refinance risk and improving pro forma confidence.

stories.title: Cybersecurity Tracker SecurityScorecard Renews 1140 Avenue of the Americas Lease
stories.excerpt: A cybersecurity risk management firm is renewing its Midtown office space, Commercial Observer has learned. SecurityScorecard signed a five-year renewal on its 8,475-square-foot space at 1140 Avenue of the Americas, owned by American Strategic Investment Company, where it has been since 2023, according to tenant broker JLL. The asking rent was not immediately disclosed, but the average office asking rent in Midtown in the second quarter of 2026 was $86.18 per square foot, according to a CBRE report. “SecurityScorecard is experiencing tremendous momentum as organizations around the world increasingly rely on our platform to manage cyber risk across their digital ecosystems,” Aleksandr Yampolskiy, CEO and founder of SecurityScorecard, said in a statement. “Renewing our headquarters at 1140 Avenue of the Americas reflects our long-term commitment to the city and provides our team with a workplace that supports continued growth, innovation and collaboration.” JLL’s Valentin Stobetsky negotiated on behalf of the tenant, while Josh Kuriloff, Matthias Li, Heather Thomas, Pierce Hance and Nicole Estevez of Cushman & Wakefield handled the deal for the landlord. “It has a premier Midtown location, outstanding transit access, modern amenities and a unique full-floor office with an expansive private outdoor terrace that enhances the employee experience,” Stobetsky said in a statement. Li echoed the sentiment that the Midtown market and the building’s premium offerings would aid the company in its expansion. C&W did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment. The landlord, which also goes by American Realty Capital New York City REIT or New York City REIT, arranged a lease at the same tower for Epic Insurance in February, when the company took 25,500 square feet. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: SecurityScorecard renewed 8,475 SF at 1140 Avenue of the Americas, Midtown, 5-year lease.
Asking rent ~$86.18/SF (Q2 2026 Midtown average); cybersecurity firm citing growth momentum.
CEO statement emphasizes long-term commitment to NYC and team expansion.
stories.summary: SecurityScorecard, a cybersecurity risk management firm, signed a five-year lease renewal on its 8,475-square-foot headquarters at 1140 Avenue of the Americas in Midtown Manhattan, where it has been since 2023. The asking rent was approximately $86.18 per square foot, in line with Q2 2026 Midtown averages. The company's CEO cited strong growth momentum and described the renewal as reflecting long-term commitment to New York and support for continued innovation and team expansion.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact to multifamily development. Office lease renewals in Midtown do not signal residential demand; strong office tenant retention actually competes for prime NYC real estate capital and may cap residential appreciation in overlapping submarkets.

stories.title: Hilton-Branded Hotel Offerings to Anchor Former Nashville Office Tower
stories.excerpt: Office space in the downtown Fifth Third Center is slated to be converted into hundreds of hotel and timeshare units. The Nashville Business Journal reports that the rooms will be part of Hilton’s LXR Hotels & Resorts brand and Hilton Grand Vacations. Pivot Real Estate Partners and Hastings Architecture are helming the conversion of the 30-story tower. The tower, located at 424 Church St., is slated to offer a total of 483 rooms, including 318 hotel rooms and 165 timeshare units. Other features of the future hotel and timeshare tower include separate amenity spaces for hotel guests and timeshare owners, as well as a ballroom. A lobby bar, all-day restaurant and retail and coffee space are planned for the building’s ground level. The building’s plaza is planned to feature an outdoor bar with a food-and-beverage concept. Pivot Real Estate Partners bought Fifth Third Center for $55.25 million last August. The post Hilton-Branded Hotel Offerings to Anchor Former Nashville Office Tower appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Pivot Real Estate converting 30-story Fifth Third Center to 483 hotel/timeshare units, Nashville downtown.
318 hotel rooms (LXR Hotels) + 165 Hilton Grand Vacations timeshare units, purchased $55.25M Aug 2025.
Redevelopment includes separate amenities, ballroom, F&B, ground-level retail, plaza bar.
stories.summary: Pivot Real Estate Partners is converting the 30-story Fifth Third Center at 424 Church St. in downtown Nashville into 483 hotel and timeshare units comprising 318 rooms under the LXR Hotels & Resorts brand and 165 Hilton Grand Vacations timeshare units. Pivot acquired the building for $55.25 million in August 2025. The conversion includes separate amenity spaces for hotel and timeshare guests, a ballroom, ground-level retail, and an outdoor plaza bar with F&B.
stories.impact: Office-to-hotel conversion removes potential multifamily opportunity in downtown Nashville but signals strong tourism/hospitality demand and downtown activation; indicates downtown value capture flowing to hotels rather than residential. For multifamily developers: downtown Nashville residential demand may be less compelling than suburban/emerging submarkets; focus acquisition on neighborhoods with residential-favorable zoning and less hotel competition.

stories.title: Arrow Adds Veteran Multifamily Lender Ari Mandelbaum to Grow Platform
stories.excerpt: Arrow Real Estate Advisors continues to ramp up its roster nearly two years after its founding. The capital markets advisory firm founded by Morris Betesh in fall 2024 has added Ari Mandelbaum, a former lender at Greystone and Dwight Capital, as a director to help grow its multifamily debt placement business, Commercial Observer has learned. “Ari brings a highly valuable perspective to Arrow given his extensive experience on the lender side of the business,” Betesh said in a statement. “His understanding of underwriting, credit and execution allows him to approach financing assignments from both sides of the table and provide clients with a deeper level of insight throughout the capital-raising process.” Mandelbaum previously held senior roles at Greystone and Dwight Capital specializing in agency and bridge loans across multifamily and other property sectors. He was at Greystone from 2011 to 2014 before a decade-long run at Dwight, where he ascended to an executive vice president role. At Arrow, Mandelbaum will focus heavily on negotiating multifamily loans while helping borrowers navigate alternative strategies. Among the multifamily deals he originated at Dwight was a $36 million bridge loan in 2023 for Latco Enterprises to refinance its Villa Annette Apartments property in Moreno Valley, Calif., CO first reported at the time. “I’m excited to join Arrow and work alongside a team with a strong track record across the commercial real estate capital markets,” Mandelbaum said in a statement. “My experience on the credit side has given me a firsthand understanding of how transactions are evaluated, structured and executed, and I look forward to applying that perspective to help Arrow’s clients navigate increasingly structured financing environments.” The addition of Mandelbaum comes on the heels of Arrow hiring Jeff Weinberg from Meridian Capital Group as a managing director, CO previously reported. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Arrow Real Estate Advisors hired Ari Mandelbaum (ex-Greystone, Dwight Capital) as director.
Mandelbaum: 3 years Greystone (2011–2014), 10 years Dwight EVP role, agency/bridge multifamily expertise.
Arrow founded fall 2024 by Morris Betesh; now ramping multifamily debt placement platform.
stories.summary: Arrow Real Estate Advisors, a capital markets advisory firm founded by Morris Betesh in fall 2024, has added Ari Mandelbaum as director to expand its multifamily debt placement business. Mandelbaum previously held senior roles at Greystone (2011–2014) and Dwight Capital (2014–2024), where he rose to executive vice president specializing in agency and bridge loans across multifamily and other sectors. At Arrow, he will focus on multifamily loan negotiation and alternative financing strategies.
stories.impact: New debt placement platforms hiring experienced lenders from agency and bridge shops signals capital market fragmentation and rising demand for alternative debt structures outside traditional agency channels. Multifamily developers should monitor Arrow's growth and loan offerings; alternative lenders with ex-agency expertise may offer faster execution and creative structuring for transitional or non-conforming deals as agency lending tightens.

stories.title: Florida Tech Opens $96 Million Student Dorm
stories.excerpt: Florida Tech has opened the doors of a six-story, 556-bed student housing complex on the Melbourne campus. It was funded through $96.1 million in municipal bond financing. Dubbed Crimson Crossing, it was built using a Public-Private Partnership (P3) model with Servitas Development. It took 15 months to build. The majority of the apartment-style units in the complex will be four-bedroom, two-bathroom suites equipped with full kitchens. Amenities will include a classroom area, study and lounge spaces, a multipurpose room and two outdoor courtyards designed for dining and recreation. The need for more student housing is fueled by Florida Tech’s growing student body. Traditional and online student enrollment has increased more than 27% since 2019, reaching over 10,000 students in fall 2025. During that same timeframe, first-time-in-college students have jumped over 43%, and the fall-to-fall retention rate increased from 74.3% in 2022 to 83.3% in 2025. The post Florida Tech Opens $96 Million Student Dorm appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Florida Tech opened 556-bed student housing (Crimson Crossing) via $96.1M municipal bond financing.
6-story complex built in 15 months via P3 model with Servitas; majority 4-bed, 2-bath suites.
Enrollment +27% since 2019 (10,000+ students fall 2025); first-time students +43%, retention 83.3%.
stories.summary: Florida Tech opened Crimson Crossing, a 556-bed, six-story student housing complex on its Melbourne campus, funded through $96.1 million in municipal bond financing via a Public-Private Partnership with Servitas Development. Construction took 15 months. The complex features primarily four-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment-style units with full kitchens, plus study spaces, multipurpose room, and outdoor courtyards. Florida Tech's student enrollment has grown over 27% since 2019 to 10,000+ students, with first-time-in-college enrollment up 43% and fall-to-fall retention at 83.3% as of fall 2025.
stories.impact: No direct multifamily impact. Student housing is distinct asset class with different financing, operations, and tenant base. However, 27% enrollment growth in Melbourne signals robust demand drivers (population, job growth, institutional investment) that may support adjacent multifamily development if market permits it; monitor whether Florida Tech expansion catalyzes broader residential growth in Space Coast submarket.

stories.title: The Fever’s Down, But New York’s Rent-Stabilized Market Is Still Ill
stories.excerpt: New York City’s rent-stabilized housing stock has an increasingly serious economic problem. For years, the operating expenses of these buildings have been rising much faster than their revenues. Insurance premiums, real estate taxes, water and sewer charges, fuel, labor, repairs and maintenance have all increased significantly, while the ability of owners to increase rents has been severely constrained. The Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act of 2019 eliminated or restricted many of the mechanisms owners previously used to recover investments in their buildings, and now we have a rent freeze layered on top of that. The result is not complicated. When expenses consistently grow faster than revenue, eventually the two lines cross. Robert Knakal. PHOTO: Patrick McMullan/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images New York City’s Article XI is increasingly being discussed as one possible solution. The program can provide an extraordinary property-tax benefit to qualifying buildings for as long as 40 years, replacing conventional real estate taxes with a substantially lower PILOT, or payment in lieu of taxes. For a distressed rent-stabilized building, the impact can be dramatic. A building paying 25 percent or more of its gross revenue in real estate taxes might see that burden reduced substantially. Suddenly, a property that was barely breaking even, or even losing money, can generate positive cash flow again. For an owner facing a mortgage maturity, foreclosure or the prospect of handing the keys back to the lender, Article XI can be a lifeline. But a lifeline is not a cure. Think about a patient suffering from a serious infection and running a dangerously high fever. You give the patient Tylenol. The fever comes down. The patient feels better. Everyone is relieved. bullets: NYC rent-stabilized buildings: operating expenses rising faster than constrained rents; rent freeze in effect.
2019 Housing Stability Act eliminated recovery mechanisms; insurance, taxes, labor, fuel costs surging.
Article XI PILOT program cited as distressed-building solution; can reduce tax burden dramatically over 40 years.
stories.summary: New York City's rent-stabilized housing stock faces a structural economic problem: operating expenses (insurance, real estate taxes, water, sewer, fuel, labor, maintenance) are rising much faster than revenues. The 2019 Housing Stability and Tenant Protection Act eliminated mechanisms owners used to recover capital investments, and a rent freeze has now been layered on top. The result is negative cash flow spread that will eventually force distress. Article XI, a program offering substantially lower PILOTs (payments in lieu of taxes) for up to 40 years, is being discussed as a potential solution.
stories.impact: Rent-stabilized portfolio distress in NYC creates neither development nor acquisition opportunity for market-rate developers—regulatory risk and capital intensity are prohibitive. However, if Article XI adoption accelerates or rent-freeze policies change, stabilized-to-market conversions or ground-lease repositioning could unlock value. For now, focus capital on free-market multifamily; stabilized stock will likely face owner capitulation or public intervention, not private investment.

stories.title: 107-Unit Charleston BTR Community Trades for $32M
stories.excerpt: Blaze Capital Partners offloaded the Charleston Row Townhomes, a 107-unit townhome property in Pineville, North Carolina. Blaze Capital Partners and Argosy Real Estate Partners acquired the asset in July 2022 for $32 million. The property was 98% occupied at the time of sale. Berkadia’s Caleb Troop, Thomas Colaiezzi and Matt Robertson and Drew Kwiatkowski of Berkadia Charlotte led the sale on Blaze Capital. The buyer was not disclosed. Located at 11945 Crooked Stick Place and built in 1969, the community offers two- and three-bedroom townhome units, with sizes ranging from 1,162 to over 1,700 square feet. Rents range from$1,725-$2,675. The townhome residences feature private patios and private one- or two-car garages. Charleston Row Townhomes is strategically located in Pineville within Charlotte’s highly sought-after South Charlotte corridor, placing residents in the heart of an employment-rich and amenity-driven submarket. bullets: Blaze Capital offloaded Charleston Row Townhomes (107 units) in Pineville, Charlotte South; $32M sale.
Built 1969; 2–3 bed townhomes, 1,162–1,700 SF, rents $1,725–$2,675; 98% occupied at sale.

stories.summary: Blaze Capital Partners sold Charleston Row Townhomes, a 107-unit townhome community in Pineville, North Carolina (South Charlotte corridor), for $32 million. The property, built in 1969, offers two- and three-bedroom units ranging from 1,162 to over 1,700 square feet, with rents between $1,725 and $2,675. The asset was 98% occupied at sale. Blaze and co-owner Argosy Real Estate Partners had acquired the property in July 2022 for the same $32 million purchase price.
stories.impact: No price appreciation over 4-year hold despite 98% occupancy and rent growth environment signals South Charlotte submarket saturation or cap-rate compression limiting returns. For developers: townhome product in mature Charlotte South submarkets faces competitive pressure and limited upside; focus new supply on emerging South Charlotte nodes (Ballantyne, Weddington) or alternative product types (garden-style, Class A mid-rise) where supply gaps remain.

stories.title: Every Industry Eventually Learns a Shared Language. Data Centers Are Next.
stories.excerpt: One question has stayed with me since my last column on data center disclosure: How do standards emerge in an industry where every project is different? It is an important question because nothing about today’s data center market looks standardized. Every project is different. Every community asks different questions. Every developer tells a slightly different story. Yet history suggests that industries almost never begin with standards. They grow into them. Suhail Y Tayeb. PHOTO: Courtesy NYU The reason is straightforward. As industries mature, inconsistent information becomes expensive. Investors, lenders, insurers, regulators and customers all reach the same conclusion. Comparing projects is easier when everyone speaks the same language. The pattern repeats itself across industries. Finance eventually adopted Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) because investors needed confidence that financial statements meant the same thing from one company to the next. The standards did not make companies identical. They made companies comparable. Real estate followed a similar path. Residential appraisers do not prepare a different report for every lender. Standardized appraisal forms such as the Uniform Residential Appraisal Report, also known as Form 1004, became common because investors buying mortgages needed comparable information. The form did not standardize houses. It standardized how houses were described. Green building tells the same story. LEED began as a voluntary certification developed by the U.S. Green Building Council. Developers pursued certification because tenants, investors and lenders increasingly viewed it as a credible signal of quality and performance. Only later did many municipalities incorporate LEED into procurement requirements, incentives and public policy. bullets: Industry opinion: data center market lacks standardized metrics; every project treated uniquely.
Historical pattern: industries mature by adopting shared disclosure standards (GAAP in finance, appraisal forms in real estate).
Data center sector approaching standardization phase; implications for comparability, investor/lender confidence, valuation.
stories.summary: An opinion column argues that the data center market currently lacks standardized disclosure metrics and reporting frameworks, making project-by-project comparison difficult for investors, lenders, and regulators. The author draws parallels to how finance adopted GAAP and real estate developed standardized appraisal forms, noting that industries typically mature by establishing shared languages and measurement standards. The column suggests data centers are approaching a similar inflection point where standardization will emerge to enable comparison and reduce information asymmetry.
stories.impact: Indirect signal for multifamily developers: if data center standardization accelerates, it could reshape real estate capital allocation, lender risk models, and competitive positioning for land/development capital in core markets (Texas, Phoenix, Virginia). Standardization may also increase data center project financing efficiency, crowding out alternative real estate sectors from marginal lending capacity; watch for tightening multifamily debt availability as lenders focus on newer, standardized asset classes.

stories.title: New York City’s Next Multifamily Shortage? Buildings to Buy.
stories.excerpt: For years, nearly every conversation about New York City multifamily has centered around one shortage: housing. We don’t have enough apartments. We don’t build fast enough. Vacancy remains tight, construction is expensive, and the regulatory environment makes adding new supply increasingly difficult. But there is another shortage developing that investors and owners should be paying close attention to: a shortage of multifamily buildings to buy. I am talking about quality buildings worth buying — free-market apartment buildings with minimal regulatory risk hurdles. Lev Mavashev. PHOTO: Courtesy Alpha Realty That may sound strange after several years when buyers had the upper hand and plenty of owners struggled to get their pricing. But the market is changing. Capital is coming back faster than quality inventory is coming to market, and the numbers are starting to reflect that. According to Alpha Realty’s second-quarter 2026 multifamily market report, New York City recorded 304 multifamily transactions during the three months ended June 30, up 10.5 percent from the first quarter and 2.4 percent year-over-year. That followed 275 transactions in the first quarter, which itself was up nearly 20 percent from the prior year. In other words, despite elevated borrowing costs, transaction velocity continues to improve. Most of the multifamily transactions have been for free-market and newer construction buildings. What’s interesting is that multifamily buildings with 20-plus units accounted for 112 transactions in the second quarter, up 24.4 percent from the quarter before and 8.7 percent from a year earlier. Those assets represented $872.2 million, or roughly 57 percent of all New York City multifamily dollar volume during the quarter. That follows an already strong first quarter, when properties with at least 20 units accounted for $1.06 billion, or approximately 61 percent of citywide multifamily volume. bullets: NYC multifamily market now facing inventory shortage (not housing shortage): quality free-market buildings scarce.
Q2 2026: 304 transactions (+10.5% QoQ, +2.4% YoY); capital inflow faster than quality inventory supply.
Buyers gaining upper hand again after years of owner-favorable conditions; traditional pricing power eroding.
stories.summary: New York City's multifamily market is experiencing a new scarcity: a shortage of quality free-market apartment buildings available to purchase, rather than a shortage of housing units per se. According to Alpha Realty's Q2 2026 report, NYC recorded 304 multifamily transactions in the three months ended June 30 (up 10.5% QoQ and 2.4% YoY), signaling strong buyer activity. Capital is flowing back into the market faster than quality, minimally regulated inventory is coming to market, shifting negotiating power back toward buyers and creating pricing pressure on sellers.
stories.impact: Critical signal for NYC multifamily developers and acquirers: institutional capital is re-entering the market, and per-unit pricing for quality stabilized assets is likely to compress as competition intensifies and supply remains constrained. Developers with free-market, low-regulatory-risk assets should execute sales/recaps now before cap rates compress further. Conversely, if seeking to acquire, expect prolonged negotiation and bidding wars; focus on value-add and development opportunities where fewer buyers compete.
